chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Sovereign Debt Actually Is

lessons.title: Case Study: India's Own Borrowing Programme, from RBI Auctions to RBI Retail Direct

children.text: Three lessons in, you understand why India borrows, who lends, and how to read the numbers. This closing lesson of the chapter puts all of it together by walking through the actual machinery: how the RBI runs a G-Sec auction, what instruments the government actually issues, and how, since 2021, an ordinary investor with a PAN card and Rs 10,000 can participate directly, something that was simply not possible a decade ago.
The Borrowing Calendar: How India Plans Its Debt Issuance

India does not raise its full annual borrowing in one lump sum. The RBI, in consultation with the government, publishes a half yearly borrowing calendar, one for April to September (H1) and one for October to March (H2), specifying the approximate amount to be borrowed, the auction dates, and often the tenor buckets the government intends to issue into. This predictability is deliberate. It lets banks, insurers, and other large investors plan their own cash flows around known auction dates rather than being surprised by ad hoc issuance, which in turn keeps the market calmer and the government's borrowing cost lower than it would otherwise be.

children.text: On an auction day, the RBI announces a notified amount, say Rs 30,000 crore of a specific bond. Bids come in through two channels.

For benchmark dated securities, the RBI generally uses the uniform price method, meaning every successful bidder, whether competitive or non-competitive, pays the same cut-off price corresponding to the same cut-off yield, not whatever price they individually bid.

Take an illustrative example. Suppose the RBI notifies Rs 30,000 crore of a new 10-year benchmark bond, and total bids received across all participants add up to Rs 90,000 crore. That gives a bid-to-cover ratio of 3, a rough gauge of how hungry the market is for that paper: the higher the ratio, the stronger the demand, and generally the lower the cut-off yield the government has to accept. If the auction settles at a cut-off yield of 7.02%, that yield becomes the benchmark 10-year rate quoted across financial media and used to price everything from corporate bonds to floating rate loans that day.

body.title: Calculate the Bid-to-Cover Ratio
body.prompt: The RBI notifies Rs 25,000 crore of a new dated G-Sec. Total bids received across competitive and non-competitive segments add up to Rs 87,500 crore. What is the bid-to-cover ratio?
body.explanation: Bid-to-cover ratio is simply total bids received divided by the notified (auctioned) amount: Rs 87,500 crore divided by Rs 25,000 crore equals 3.5x. A ratio comfortably above 1 signals healthy demand; ratios below 1, or a partially devolved auction where primary dealers are forced to absorb unsold paper, are a warning sign analysts watch closely.

children.text: RBI Retail Direct: Sovereign Debt Investing for Individuals

For most of India's post-liberalisation history, buying a G-Sec meant going through a bank, a mutual fund, or a broker, layers that added cost and distance between the individual saver and the government bond market. That changed in February 2021, when the RBI launched the Retail Direct scheme. Any resident individual can open a free Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account directly with the RBI, using nothing more than a PAN, a bank account, and a mobile number, and from there place non-competitive bids in primary auctions of T-Bills, dated G-Secs, SDLs, and SGBs, or buy and sell in the secondary market through the NDS-OM platform. There is no fee for opening or maintaining the account, and the minimum investment in most primary auctions is Rs 10,000.

body.label: RBI Retail Direct Portal
body.description: Open a free Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account to bid in primary G-Sec, T-Bill, SDL, and SGB auctions, or trade in the secondary market, directly with the RBI.

body.text: Retail Direct does not change the underlying risk of a G-Sec, sovereign risk is still sovereign risk, but it does remove the layer of intermediary cost and access that used to separate individual investors from the same instruments banks and insurers were buying all along. It is also a small but real widening of India's domestic investor base, the same captive-demand story from the previous lesson, just extended one level further down.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What is the main practical difference between a competitive bid and a non-competitive bid in a G-Sec auction?
options: Competitive bids are only for foreign investors; non-competitive bids are only for Indian residents
A competitive bid specifies a price or yield the bidder wants; a non-competitive bid simply accepts whatever yield the auction settles at
Non-competitive bids earn a higher guaranteed return than competitive bids
There is no real difference, the terms are interchangeable
body.explanation: Competitive bidders, mainly large institutions and primary dealers, name the price or yield they are willing to accept, and the RBI fills the notified amount starting from the most aggressive bids. Non-competitive bidders, a route commonly used by retail investors through RBI Retail Direct, agree upfront to accept the cut-off yield the auction produces, without having to guess or negotiate a price themselves.

body.text: The same government bond market that only banks, insurers, and large institutions could access for most of India's history is now a few clicks away from any resident individual with a PAN card and Rs 10,000. The instruments and the risk have not changed. Who can reach them has.

children.text: That closes out how sovereign debt actually gets created, sold, and held in India's own case. The next chapter turns outward, to how the market and rating agencies size up a country's creditworthiness once that debt exists: the economic, political, and currency risk framework that sits behind every sovereign credit rating and every basis point of spread an investor demands.

points: India borrows on a published half-yearly calendar (H1 and H2), giving the market advance notice of auction dates and amounts, which helps keep borrowing costs lower and more predictable.

G-Sec auctions combine competitive bidding, mainly by banks, insurers, and primary dealers, with non-competitive bidding reserved for smaller investors; benchmark auctions typically use the uniform price method, so all successful bidders receive the same cut-off yield.
India's sovereign debt toolkit includes T-Bills (short-term, discount instruments), dated G-Secs (the main workhorse), floating rate bonds, state government SDLs, and Sovereign Gold Bonds.

Since February 2021, RBI Retail Direct lets any resident individual open a free gilt account and access primary auctions and secondary market trading directly, with a minimum investment of Rs 10,000 in most auctions.
Retail access does not change the underlying sovereign risk of a G-Sec, it changes who can reach the same instruments institutions have always held.

body.text: The borrowing figures, auction mechanics, and instrument details in this lesson are approximate and based on recent RBI practice, which can and does change. Always verify current borrowing calendars, minimum investment amounts, and instrument availability on the RBI's official website or the Retail Direct portal before investing.
